title: The 48 Laws of Power II in Leadership
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain reinterprets Robert Greene's The 48 Laws of Power for managers, arguing that power dynamics shape promotions, approvals and influence whether or not leaders acknowledge them. His organising move is to sort all 48 laws into five sources of power: positional, relational, insight, execution and adaptive. Each source is introduced with how it shows up in organisational life, and each law is then softened into a workplace interpretation with a concrete example, often recasting Greene's harsher maxims as matters of emotional intelligence, timing or direct conflict resolution. Positional power is presented as getting a leader into the room but not keeping people listening, while relational power is said to shape more decisions than org charts. Insight and execution power stress timing, restraint and results over argument, and adaptive power emphasises reinvention and paced change. The piece closes by insisting that readers need not endorse every law but should stop pretending the game of power does not exist.
points: Jain's distinctive contribution is a taxonomy that maps Greene's 48 laws onto five sources of leadership power: positional, relational, insight, execution and adaptive.
Positional power is treated as necessary but insufficient; title gets a leader into the room, but reputation, presence and confidence decide whether people keep listening.
Relational power is said to shape more decisions than org charts, with laws on self-interest, observation and knowing people's pressure points reframed as emotional intelligence.
Insight and execution power favour timing, saying less and letting results settle arguments, on the claim that people respect results more than rhetoric.
Adaptive power covers addressing blockers directly and pacing change, warning that reforming too much at once triggers change fatigue.
quotes: Robert Greene’s The 48 Laws of Power, one of my favorite books about human psychology, cuts through the corporate fluff and reveals the real game leaders are playing. And if you’re leading, you’re already playing the game — whether you realize it or not.

But while it can get you in the room, it won’t keep people listening. These laws help you protect your reputation, project confidence, and show up like someone whose presence carries weight — even when your title isn’t enough.
In every organization, relationships shape more decisions than org charts do. This is the power of who knows you, who trusts you, and who’s willing to go to bat for you.
These small acts make people lower their guard. When you surprise people with kindness or openness, you shift the power dynamic. It's not manipulation — it's emotional intelligence.
A brilliant idea delivered too early gets rejected. The right solution pushed too late feels irrelevant. Timing is the hidden layer of leadership.
It’s not enough to have a vision — you have to make it happen. These laws remind you that people respect results more than rhetoric.
Leadership isn’t just about vision and values. It’s about understanding power — how it moves, how it shifts, and how to use it without losing yourself.
